title: Standing stones at Avebury in Wiltshire, England
desc: As morning mist drifts among the standing stones of Avebury in Wiltshire, England, the scene feels almost timeless. These ancient megaliths form part of one of the world's most remarkable prehistoric landscapes, centred on a vast Neolithic monument built around 4,500 years ago. Avebury contains the world's largest prehistoric stone circle, as well as a massive henge and stone avenues extending into the surrounding countryside. Together with nearby monuments such as Silbury Hill and West Kennet Avenue, it forms part of an extensive Neolithic complex that has fascinated generations of visitors, researchers and archaeologists.

title: Kunětická hora Castle, Bohemia, Czechia
desc: What stories could these walls tell? Rising above eastern Bohemia in Czechia, Kunětická hora Castle has witnessed centuries of history. Dating to the late 14th century, the castle gradually evolved into an impressive fortress and noble residence. Its elevated position offered commanding views of the surrounding countryside and helped make it an important stronghold.

title: A grove of pond cypress trees with autumn foliage, Georgia, United States
desc: Reflected in calm water and glowing in the light of the setting sun, this grove of pond cypress creates a striking display of colour and symmetry. Native to the southeastern United States, the species is associated with shallow ponds, depressions and wetland habitats. This image was captured in Georgia, where these trees can be found in places such as the Okefenokee Swamp and other low-lying wetlands.
main_text: Pond cypress can develop knobby root structures known as 'knees' that rise above the water or soil around the tree.

title: Autumn waterfalls near Sitovo, Plovdiv Province, Bulgaria
desc: In Bulgaria's Western Rhodope Mountains, autumn leaves gather beside the rushing waters of Sitovo Waterfall. Near the village of Sitovo, southwest of Plovdiv, the falls tumble beneath an old stone bridge whose arch frames the cascades like a storybook scene. Moss-covered stones and pine trees add shades of green to the autumn landscape, while fallen leaves gather along the water's edge or drift through its pools. The falls become especially lively after rain and during spring snowmelt, when the surrounding woodland echoes with the sound of rushing water.

head_line: The road that runs on water
title: Grand Canal in Venice, Italy
desc: What if a city's busiest street had no road? In Venice, Italy, traffic flows along the Grand Canal, a 3.9-kilometre waterway that winds through the city in a giant reverse S-shape. Known to locals as the Canalazzo, it is Venice's main water-traffic corridor, carrying vaporetti, water taxis, gondolas, police boats and other vessels. The canal follows the course of an ancient river that once flowed into the Venetian Lagoon.

title: Royal Portuguese Cabinet of Reading, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil
desc: Today we're inside the Royal Portuguese Cabinet of Reading in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, where the humble act of opening a book took on grand architectural ambitions. Founded in 1837 by 43 Portuguese immigrants, just 15 years after Brazil's independence, the institution eventually moved into the building seen here, completed half a century later in a lavish Neo-Manueline style. Shelves soar over 20 metres around a vast reading room, crowned by a monumental stained-glass skylight that makes daylight part of the design.

title: Two grey wolves, Yellowstone National Park, Wyoming, United States
desc: Two grey wolves move through the sagebrush of Yellowstone National Park in Wyoming, home to some of North America's most closely watched wolf packs. Their thick coats help them withstand harsh winters, and their keen senses make them skilled hunters and communicators.
main_text: Grey wolves can communicate through howls, body language, scent marking and a range of vocalisations, including barks, whines and growls.

title: Autumn in Naejangsan National Park, South Korea
desc: Few places in South Korea capture the magic of autumn quite like Naejangsan National Park, where mountainsides glow in brilliant shades of scarlet, orange, yellow and gold. Located in the country's southwest, the park is particularly famous for its vivid maple colours, making it one of Korea's premier destinations for autumn scenery. Its name, meaning 'many secrets in the mountains,' reflects the varied landscapes found throughout the region.

title: Nguyen Hoang Bridge over the Perfume River, Hue, Vietnam
desc: Bridging the gap between old and new, Nguyen Hoang Bridge gives Hue's skyline a fresh connection. Spanning the Perfume River in Vietnam, the modern steel-arch landmark opened to traffic on 26 March 2025. Its design, called 'The Crane Facing Thien Mu,' draws inspiration from a local legend and nearby Thien Mu Pagoda.

title: Brown-throated sloth, Puerto Viejo de Talamanca, Costa Rica
desc: Slow and steady wins the race—and the brown-throated sloth seems perfectly happy to skip the race altogether. On International Sloth Day, this three-toed mammal offers a different lesson in getting by: conserve energy, hang on and take your time.

title: Goddess Durga idol in a pandal
desc: Nine days of devotion, nine forms of Durga and one powerful finale—Maha Navami brings Navratri to its most intense stretch. Observed on the ninth day, it celebrates Goddess Durga's victory over the buffalo demon Mahishasura, earning her the name Mahishasuramardini, or slayer of Mahishasura. The day is also dedicated to Maa Siddhidatri, the ninth form of Navadurga, who is associated with spiritual powers and blessings.
main_text: A 41.5-metre-tall Durga Puja pandal, modelled on Vrindavan's Chandrodaya Temple, earned a Guinness World Records title as the tallest pandal ever built.

title: Dolbadarn Castle, Llanberis, Eryri National Park (Snowdonia), Wales
desc: If parks could keep birthday diaries, Eryri National Park (Snowdonia) in Wales would have quite the story to tell. The park turns 75 today, marking the anniversary of its designation in 1951. Eryri stretches across more than 2,100 square kilometres, with nine mountain ranges, about 120 kilometres of coastline and habitats ranging from peatlands and native woodlands to upland landscapes. At more than 1,000 metres, Yr Wyddfa is Eryri's highest point. Nearby, the Carneddau and Glyderau add their own peaks, while Cadair Idris rises in the south. These protected landscapes provide habitats for wildlife and include 17 National Nature Reserves and 56 Sites of Special Scientific Interest.

title: Life-size replica of Chauvet cave art in Vallon-Pont-d'Arc, France
desc: Some discoveries start with a shovel. Others start with a drawing on a cave wall. International Archaeology Day celebrates both the detective work and the evidence behind them. Organised by the Archaeological Institute of America, this annual event began in 2011 and became International Archaeology Day in 2013 as participation expanded worldwide. Today, it brings archaeology closer to the public through talks, museum programmes, site visits, simulated digs and hands-on activities.
main_text: The Chauvet Cave preserves the footprints of a prehistoric adolescent who walked barefoot through its passages about 30,000 years ago.

title: Mount Sneffels in the San Juan Mountains near Ridgway, Colorado, United States
desc: Some mountains make you work for the view. Mount Sneffels makes you work for the last few hundred feet. Rising to 4,313 metres in Colorado's San Juan Mountains in the United States, this fourteener is a familiar sight around Ridgway, Ouray and Telluride. It sits within the 16,587-acre (6,713-hectare) Mount Sneffels Wilderness, a protected area designated in 1980. Hikers can reach the mountain from several approaches, including the Yankee Boy Basin and the Blue Lakes area.

title: View of the Wroclaw Market Square from the Witches' Bridge in Wroclaw, Poland
desc: As twilight settles over Wroclaw, golden light spills across rooftops, church towers and one of Central Europe's most striking historic centres. This southwestern Polish city spans islands and waterways linked by more than 100 bridges, blending medieval architecture with vibrant modern life. At its heart is Rynek, a lively Market Square established in the 13th century and home to the Gothic Old Town Hall, one of Wroclaw's most recognisable landmarks.

title: Ammonite fossils from the Jurassic Period
desc: How do we know what Earth looked like long before humans appeared? Fossils provide many clues. From dinosaurs to tiny marine organisms, these remnants of the past preserve snapshots of ancient worlds that no longer exist.
main_text: A fossil doesn't have to be a bone. Tracks, burrows, nests and other traces of ancient life can become fossils too.

head_line: A symphony in blue and green
title: Plitvice Lakes National Park, Croatia
desc: Water seems to be everywhere at Plitvice Lakes National Park in Croatia. Sixteen terraced lakes are linked by a network of waterfalls, streams and cascades that wind through forested limestone canyons. The constantly changing colours of the water, ranging from emerald green to deep blue, are shaped by minerals, sunlight and ever-changing reflections. Established in 1949, Plitvice Lakes is Croatia's oldest and largest national park. The landscape is famous for its tufa barriers, natural limestone formations created as mineral-rich water deposits calcium carbonate over centuries. These barriers continue to grow and change, gradually transforming the park's waterfalls and lakes.

title: Mumbles Pier, Swansea, Wales
desc: What do you get when a railway, a lifeboat station and a seaside day out meet at the water's edge? Mumbles Pier. Stretching 255 metres into Swansea Bay, this Victorian landmark opened on 10 May 1898 and has been part of the Welsh coast ever since.

title: Glade Creek Grist Mill, Babcock State Park, West Virginia, United States
desc: Surrounded by a patchwork of red, orange and gold, Glade Creek Grist Mill stands above the rocky waters of Glade Creek in West Virginia's Babcock State Park, United States. Although it looks like a relic from the pioneer era, the mill is actually a carefully crafted tribute to Appalachia's milling heritage.

title: Double-crested cormorants over Monterey Bay, California, United States
desc: World Migratory Bird Day celebrates one of nature's greatest journeys. Observed each year in May and October, the global campaign reflects migration patterns around the world and highlights the importance of protecting the habitats and flyways that birds depend on. 'Every Bird Counts—Your Observations Matter!' is the 2026 theme, emphasising how observations by individuals and communities can contribute to bird research, monitoring and conservation, helping scientists better understand migration.
main_text: Bird migration can take many forms: some birds travel north or south, while others move to different elevations or habitats.

title: View of the Sanguinaires Islands from Corsica, France
desc: Just off the coast of Corsica, France, the Sanguinaires Islands rise from the Mediterranean as a small archipelago of four rugged, rocky islands. Viewed from a historic watchtower, they sit at the entrance to the Gulf of Ajaccio. Steep cliffs, centuries-old landmarks and sweeping sea views have drawn visitors to the area for generations. Though the farthest island lies only about 2 kilometres from shore, the archipelago feels surprisingly remote, surrounded by open water and shaped by wind, waves and salt spray.

title: Octopus in defensive posture, Mayotte, Indian Ocean
desc: Something has clearly crossed a line. Off the coast of Mayotte in the Indian Ocean, this octopus has adopted a defensive posture that says: whatever is approaching should reconsider its life choices.

title: Moss-covered rocks in Puzzlewood, Forest of Dean, Gloucestershire, England
desc: What if a forest could keep you guessing at every turn? At Puzzlewood, near Coleford in the Forest of Dean, England, winding paths lead through twisted trees, moss-covered rocks and deep stone ravines. Its unusual rock formations, known as scowles, are natural geological features that were exposed and modified over time and later exploited for iron ore mining during the Roman period and possibly earlier. In 1848, a worker discovered more than 3,000 Roman-era coins hidden in earthenware jars inside a rock cavity, turning the woodland into a real-life treasure hunt.

title: Danxia landform, Zhangye National Geopark, Gansu, China
desc: What if a mountain range could show you its geological history in stripes? At Zhangye National Geopark in China, the rocks do exactly that. Ridges roll across the landscape in bands of red, orange, yellow, brown and other earthy tones. Known as the Danxia landform, this striking landscape was shaped by layers of sedimentary rock deposited over geological time. Tectonic forces later lifted and folded the rocks, while weathering and erosion carved them into ridges, cliffs, gullies and peaks.

title: Adélie penguins, Antarctica
desc: What can a 70-centimetre-tall bird teach us about life? Quite a lot. The Adélie penguin offers a lesson plan packed with resourcefulness, resilience and a little mischief. Found along the Antarctic coast, the species was named after Adèle, the wife of French explorer Jules Dumont d'Urville, during the expedition that encountered the penguins in 1840.
main_text: Adélie penguins do not have teeth, but instead have sharp, backward-pointing spikes called papillae on their tongues and the roofs of their mouths.

title: Artemis I moon rocket at Launch Complex 39B, Kennedy Space Center, Florida, United States
desc: First, you build a rocket. Then you ask it to leave Earth, fly to the moon, survive the trip and bring its spacecraft home. Simple, right? Well, not quite. World Space Week, observed every 4-10 October, celebrates the science that makes missions like this possible. The United Nations established the observance in 1999 to commemorate Sputnik 1's launch on 4 October 1957, and the entry into force of the Outer Space Treaty on 10 October 1967. This year's theme, 'Rocket Revolution,' focuses on the evolving technology driving space exploration.

title: Brown bear in Silver Salmon Creek, Lake Clark National Park and Preserve, Alaska, United States
desc: The season of big meals, bigger bellies and stocking up for winter is here. In Alaska, United States, brown bears at Lake Clark National Park and Preserve make the most of the food still available in October. They feed on fish, sedges, berries, roots, clams and other foods to build up fat reserves. Some can weigh more than 450 kilograms before entering their dens for hibernation. That stored fat helps them survive the winter, when they do not eat or drink.

head_line: The man who made peace powerful
title: Mahatma Gandhi statue at the Sabarmati Ashram in Ahmedabad, Gujarat
desc: Not every freedom fighter carried a weapon. He carried an idea. Gandhi Jayanti marks the birth of Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi, born in Porbandar, India, in 1869. He became a key leader of India's independence movement through satyagraha, his philosophy of truth and non-violent resistance. His 1930 Salt March showed how something as ordinary as salt could become a powerful symbol of protest. His influence eventually reached far beyond India, inspiring movements built around peaceful resistance.

head_line: Carved from two points of view
title: View into the sky from Nathmal Ki Haveli courtyard, Jaisalmer, Rajasthan
desc: What if two architects worked on the same house but saw it differently? Nathmal Ki Haveli in Jaisalmer offers the answer in carved sandstone. Built in the late 19th century, the haveli is associated with architect brothers Hathi and Lulu, who worked independently on its two sides. They look similar at first, but their fine details differ.
